title: Redwood throughput tuning - technical deep dive
summary: Technical deep dive on throughput tuning. Redwood SE walked through continuous batching and scheduler knobs (latency vs throughput tradeoffs), recommended max_num_seqs and token limits per workload, and described KV cache warmup patterns and caching strategies. Discussed quantization benefits (4-bit) and potential quality regressions, and VPC/on-prem networking considerations (eg, intra-cluster latency and HSM/KMS integration). Agreed to run a short benchmark in customer VPC, share perf spreadsheet, and follow up with tuning guide + security docs.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (BrightScale Head of ML), Oliver Grant (BrightScale SRE), Priya Rao (BrightScale Infra)

Summary (auto): go-through of continuous batching and scheduler knobs, set pilot, share docs.

[00:00:00] Lena: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'll hand over to Samir to kick off the tuning deep dive, but quick intro, i'm Lena reconciling the account and we'll own next steps
[00:00:12] Samir: yeah hi all, Samir here, i'll walk through how we tune throughput for real workloads, i'll talk continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, token limits and the kv cache behavior, and then run through config examples. if something sounds odd interrupt me.
[00:00:30] Maya: thanks, our main goal is to max throughput for batch inference (few-ms latency not required) while keeping cost predictable. we run in our VPC with granite nodes, and we have a small on-prem cluster for sensitive data.
[00:00:45] Samir: great, that's a common pattern. quick clarifier: when you say "batch inference" is that batched requests arriving in bursts or long-running streams?
[00:00:55] Oliver: mostly bursts, we get spikes from nightly jobs and some user-driven bulk jobs. Occasionally real-time chat but that's lower qps.
[00:01:12] Samir: perfect. so continuous batching is where the runtime keeps an open scheduling window to accumulate sequences into a single GPU batch; it trades a small extra tail latency for much higher throughput per token. default window is 20ms in hosted runs but in Dedicated/on-prem you can push that to 40-80ms if your SLA allows.
[00:01:36] Priya: is the 20ms number tunable per deployment? we want different settings per queue.
[00:01:44] Samir: yes, scheduler knobs are per-route. key knobs to tune: max_num_seqs (how many active sequences the scheduler will pack), max_tokens_per_batch, and scheduler_window_ms. also there's a min_batch_size to avoid tiny batches. we usually recommend starting with max_num_seqs=64 for 16GB GPU scenarios and 128 for 48GB+ when using fp16.
[00:02:10] Maya: and how do token limits interact? we often have a long prefix + short completion. will the long prefix blow up batch size?
[00:02:20] Samir: good question. token limits are enforced as two things: per-seq token cap and per-batch token cap. if a sequence has a long prefix, it consumes more computational work and larger KV cache entries; the scheduler tries to pack sequences with similar remaining length together. we also recommend a prefix bucketing strategy - route very long-context requests to a separate queue with lower max_num_seqs to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[00:02:48] [00:03:00] Oliver: any notes about KV cache warmup? we saw cold-start latencies spike for long contexts.
[00:03:06] Samir: yep, KV cache (sometimes transcribed as KV cash in our logs) warmup can be significant. warm caches reduce per-token cost and latency because the runtime avoids re-computing early layers. warmup strategies: pre-prime the cache with synthetic prefix (if you own the workload), or keep long-lived sessions pinned to specific workers (sticky routing). on Dedicated/on-prem we can also persist KV cache across requests for the same session ID if privacy rules allow.
[00:03:36] Maya: sticky routing concerns us with autoscaling, we need to keep reliability.
[00:03:42] Samir: understood. you can do soft-sticky routing: prefer same worker for affinity but fall back if capacity changes; Redwood's routing supports affinity TTLs. that gives the warm-cache benefit without hard coupling to a single host.
[00:03:58] [00:04:15] Samir: quantization discussion: 4-bit quant (Q4) gives 2-3x throughput improvement depending on kernel maturity and model topology. tradeoffs: small quality regressions for some instruction-heavy prompts; for most QA/embedding workloads it's fine. for generative dialog you should run fidelity checks. we recommend running paired benchmarks: fp16 baseline vs 4-bit to measure delta for your prompts.
[00:04:45] Priya: we have regulatory constraints; can we run 4-bit on-prem only?
[00:04:50] Samir: absolutely, Private deployments / on-prem support quantized kernels. Redwood Dedicated also supports quantization but check your compliance needs. we'll include KMS/HSM notes in the security pack.
[00:05:05] Maya: you mentioned kernel selection earlier, is that automatic?
[00:05:10] Samir: yes runtime picks kernels based on model, seq length, and hardware. there are also explicit flags if you want to pin a kernel (not typical).
[00:05:20] [00:05:40] Lena: quick interjection - Maya, you said cost predictability is a big metric, what's your target $/token or tokens/sec?
[00:05:48] Maya: ideally we want 20-30k tokens/sec aggregate for nightly jobs and each batch job shouldn't exceed a 10% variance in cost.
[00:05:58] Samir: okay that helps. tuning approach I'll suggest: 1) set scheduler_window_ms to 40ms for night batches, 2) set max_num_seqs=128 (if using 48GB GPUs) and max_tokens_per_batch to match your typical payload, 3) run a 24h throughput benchmark to capture variance.
[00:06:22] Oliver: do we need to change the model config for batching? like kv cache size or attention knobs?
[00:06:30] Samir: mostly runtime-side knobs. model config adjustments are rare but for very long contexts increase the kv_cache segment allocation. We'll provide default recommended values per model family in the guide.
[00:06:44] [00:07:00] Maya: can you explain the scheduler behavior when you hit token limits mid-batch? we've had truncated responses.
[00:07:08] Samir: when the scheduler sees a batch where some sequences exceed per-seq cap, it splits or truncates according to the policy: strict-enforce will truncate, while soft-enforce will allow completion but push sequences to next batch, increasing latency. prefer strict for predictable token accounting. we can also configure pre-scan to detect oversize sequences and route them.
[00:07:36] Priya: any cautions about autoscaling with wide scheduler windows? will it delay scale-in/out decisions?
[00:07:44] Samir: yes longer windows can mask instantaneous qps drops; autoscaling uses both queue length and worker CPU/GPU utilization signals to avoid reactionary scaling. if you want aggressive scale-down set lower affinity_ttl and shorter idle grace periods.
[00:07:58] [00:08:20] Lena: i'll pause and share a config example I put in chat - Samir can walk through it.
[00:08:26] Samir: reading it now: example route 'night-batch' -> scheduler_window_ms=50, max_num_seqs=128, max_tokens_per_batch=2048, quant=fp16 baseline and a second route 'night-batch-q4' with identical knobs but quant=4bit. run both for 24h and compare tokens/sec and p95 latency.
[00:08:54] Maya: sounds good. what do you expect for latency p95 change?
[00:08:58] Samir: for batch jobs p95 might increase by 20-40ms due to larger packing but tokens/sec typically doubles or more with quant. exacts depend on model and accelerator.
[00:09:12] [00:09:30] Oliver: network considerations - our on-prem racks have 200Gb uplinks but cross-node latency occasionally spikes. any recommended config?
[00:09:38] Samir: for on-prem/VPC, prefer colocated workers for batch-heavy jobs to reduce hop latency. also ensure RDMA or high-throughput NICs for KV cache replication if using persistent cache across nodes. we'll include a hardware checklist in the docs.
[00:09:58] Priya: is there an easy way to measure KV cache hit-rate? we want numbers to justify sticky routing.
[00:10:06] Samir: yes the runtime exports metrics: kv_cache_hit_ratio, avg_kv_items_per_session, cache_warm_time. we'll share Grafana dashboard snippets. aim for >85% hit rate for good efficiency.
[00:10:22] [00:10:40] Maya: security questions - SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS integration and audit logs. do quantization or caching affect compliance?
[00:10:48] Samir: no inherent compliance difference; the main things are data residency and key management. quantized models are just model artifacts. audit logs include cache ops and model loads. for KMS/HSM we support envelope encryption for persisted KV cache in Private. we'll attach the security pack.
[00:11:10] Lena: quick check - Priya, how much time will you need to provision a test subnet and temporary keys?
[00:11:18] Priya: we can do that in a few days, likely by 2026-05-28 if we have the spec.
[00:11:24] Lena: perfect. Samir, can you capture the exact flags to include?
[00:11:28] Samir: yes I'll add a sample config and the runbook.
[00:11:32] [00:11:50] (small crosstalk, background keyboard noise)
[00:11:58] Samir: let's talk about monitoring and cost attribution - Redwood Console gives token-level cost and per-route dashboards; for Dedicated/on-prem you can export per-worker traces. good practice is to tag routes with workload name and attach cost alerts to cumulative token burn.
[00:12:18] Maya: ok that helps. can we hook our internal billing to those tags?
[00:12:24] Lena: yes we support exporting usage to S3 or pushing to your billing system via webhook.
[00:12:30] [00:12:52] Oliver: one more deep question: max_num_seqs vs dynamic batching - what happens when you oversubscribe GPUs?
[00:12:58] Samir: oversubscribe will queue sequences and increase end-to-end latency but keep GPU utilization high. risk is OOM if max_tokens_per_batch misconfigured. we enforce hard memory guards, but you should run a stress test to find safe max_num_seqs for your model/GPU combo.
[00:13:18] Maya: do you provide pre-built stress tests?
[00:13:22] Samir: yes, we'll provide a benchmark harness and scripts that run variable qps and measure tokens/sec, p95 latency, and memory pressure.
[00:13:32] [00:13:50] (pause)
[00:13:58] Priya: latency SLOs for interactive users are 300ms p95. can we keep batch knobs separate so interactive traffic still gets low latency?
[00:14:06] Samir: absolutely, separate routes—'realtime' route uses scheduler_window_ms=5ms, min_batch_size=1, and affinity to prioritise low latency; 'bulk' route uses larger windows and higher max_num_seqs. runtime will route by route ID.
[00:14:26] Maya: about model fallback - if a quantized kernel fails do you auto-fallback to fp16?
[00:14:32] Samir: yes we have automatic fallback policies; you can set prefer_quant=false to avoid fallback or allow auto-fallback with logging.
[00:14:42] [00:15:00] Lena: jumping to next steps: i'll send the security doc and the tuning guide, Samir will attach the perf spreadsheet and runbook. Maya/Priya to provision test VPC. follow-up meeting early June.
[00:15:16] Maya: thanks, quick last Q: any gotchas about tokenization differences across frameworks? we've seen slight token counts differ.
[00:15:24] Samir: tokenization matters—use the runtime tokenization library we provide for consistency, and batch by token counts not character counts. we'll include a small utility.
[00:15:36] (meeting winds down, brief small talk)
[00:15:50] Lena: thanks everyone, we'll send notes and action items. ping us if anything urgent.
[00:16:00] (call ends)

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-transcriptions of product names (eg "KV cash"), and some speaker attribution may be simplistic (SE/AE labels).
